question: renowo ɓingel mo hakkilinta ɓingel petel hirliti ɓingel ɗo hakkilinta mai dakkere fofata nden bo fofugo ɓingel mai nda daidai ba ɓingel ɗo nda kecca ɗon ba je ɓe sakki li'al har danyugo kuma na ɓingel ɓe yiwata ɓe ndiyam fewɗum ɗume on waddata ɓingel petel fofata da kerɗo be dojjata a kai a kai bo ko haɗi fofugo mai koyi nai mo bana nane ɗume min wadata dow haala ɗo
reference:
Reenodo bingel mo hakkilinta bingel petel, hirliti bingel o hakkilinta mai daker foofata, denbo foofugo bingel mai da dedai ba.
Bingel do da chekkel don ba je be sakkiniel ha danugo, kuma naa bingel beyiiwata be diyam paudum.
Dume don waddata bingel petal foofata daker do be dojjata akai akai, bo kwadi foofugo mai hoyinai mo bana naane? Dume minwadata do halaa do?
model_answer:
A small child or infant who is breathing fast, struggling to breathe, has chest indrawing, poor feeding, fever, lethargy, convulsions, or bluish lips needs urgent assessment at a health facility the same day, because this may be pneumonia, bronchiolitis, malaria/sepsis, or another serious illness.  
Clean water or home remedies alone will not treat breathing difficulty; the child may need oxygen, antibiotics, malaria test/treatment, nebulization, or admission.  
Keep the child warm, continue breastfeeding or give small sips if able, clear the nose gently if blocked, and avoid smoke, dust, and herbal mixtures.  
Do not delay at home if the breathing is not normal or the chest is pulling in—go to the nearest hospital or emergency clinic immediately.

Mi yari sobaajo am reduujo , mo duubi mako sappo e je tati, gam o nasti dayugo bo wakati wadi . Dai min yotti sibiti mai, be hosimo bo begodimo ko haadi fu, be tawi sembe eyam mako va’e. De bawadi ko haadini fu be wada . Odo der dayugo. Odon nii har bawo awa sappo e didi. Gorko mako dayai, likita en sauri debbo mai ojaba be wanna mo CS, gam odo der dayugo do neebi .
Sobajo am salli sam , ovi wai oyidi dayugo ba roobe ibrani’en dayata .
Dagabawo o dayi bingel, bawo awaa sappo e didi o do der dayugo. Odayi bingel debbo e jamun, kuma minyettore Allah. Amma ko hilni amin bingel do wala foofa boddum. Be dimbi akai akai, marri , wugi bandu bingel do. Owooki ni amma foofugo warta deedai har jotta.

model_answer:
This sounds like birth asphyxia or serious newborn breathing difficulty after a prolonged labour/delivery.  
Whether the baby will survive and be normal depends on how long the brain lacked oxygen, the Apgar score, presence of seizures, ability to feed, blood sugar, temperature, and response to oxygen; some babies recover fully, but severe asphyxia can cause brain injury, cerebral palsy, or developmental delay.  
The baby should be managed urgently in a newborn/special care unit with oxygen or CPAP if available, warmth, glucose monitoring, treatment for possible infection, and close monitoring for seizures and feeding problems.  
If the baby is still breathing fast, turning blue, not crying well, convulsing, very weak, or unable to suck, ask for immediate referral to a higher-level hospital with neonatal care.  
After discharge, the child will need regular follow-up to check hearing, vision, movement, feeding, and developmental milestones.

model_answer:
This cough with waking at night, noisy/fast breathing or the chest/heart “beating” hard may be pneumonia, asthma/bronchiolitis, or another serious chest infection, so the child should be taken to hospital urgently—do not wait if breathing is difficult.  
Danger signs are fast breathing, chest indrawing, flaring nostrils, inability to breastfeed/drink, vomiting everything, convulsions, unusual sleepiness, blue lips, or high fever.  
While going to hospital, keep the child sitting upright, offer small frequent fluids/breastfeeding, clear the nose with saline if blocked, and give paracetamol for fever according to weight.  
Do not give cough mixtures, leftover antibiotics, or herbal mixtures, as they may harm the child or delay proper treatment.  
At the hospital they can check oxygen level and examine the chest, then give oxygen, nebulization, or antibiotics if needed.

This sounds like a seizure/convulsion with fever, which in our setting may be from severe malaria, meningitis, sepsis, low blood sugar, or a febrile convulsion, so the child should be taken to the nearest hospital immediately.  
Do not give traditional medicine, herbal mixtures, or black soap, and do not put anything in the child’s mouth during the seizure.  
Lay the child on the side, remove tight clothing, keep them away from fire/water/sharp objects, and note how long the seizure lasts.  
If the child is hot, you may tepid-sponge and give age/weight-appropriate paracetamol if awake, but do not delay going to hospital.  
Urgent treatment and tests for malaria, infection, blood sugar, and possible meningitis may be needed to prevent brain injury or death.

A child with cough and breathing difficulty for 2 months, especially worse at night, should be taken back to a hospital/paediatric clinic for full assessment, not just cough syrup.

This is an emergency after childbirth: severe weakness, dizziness/blurred vision, dry mouth/thirst may be due to dehydration, exhaustion, anemia, hidden bleeding, low blood pressure, or retained placenta.  
Take her immediately to a hospital/health centre for vital signs, examination of the womb/bleeding, blood level, IV fluids, oxytocin if needed, and possible blood transfusion.  
If the placenta has not come out within 30 minutes after birth, or bleeding starts, it is urgent and should not be managed at home.

A 7-day-old baby who cannot suck well, has noisy/difficult breathing, and milk/water seems to come through the nose needs urgent review in a hospital by a paediatrician.

Do not force breastfeeding; keep the baby upright, clear the nose gently, and give expressed breast milk in small amounts with a clean cup/spoon if the baby can swallow.  
Go immediately to emergency care if the baby is breathing fast, chest is drawing in, turns blue, is very sleepy, has fever/low temperature, or refuses feeds.

A pregnant woman of about 3 months who has lower abdominal/back pain and watery discharge should be taken to a hospital or maternity unit promptly for assessment and ultrasound scan.

Do not give herbs or strong medicines, and she should avoid sex, heavy work, and unnecessary travel until a health worker examines her.  
The doctor may do a scan, urine test, and check the cervix to know whether the pregnancy is safe and what treatment is needed.

This child must be taken urgently to a hospital for rabies post-exposure treatment, because a dog that later became abnormal/sick or died is treated as possible rabies.  
The wound should be washed well with soap and running water, and the child needs anti-rabies vaccine doses and, if the bite broke the skin, rabies immunoglobulin injected around the wound if available, plus tetanus protection and antibiotics if infected.  
It is not too late to start rabies treatment as long as the child has not developed symptoms; do not rely on traditional medicine or herbs.  
If the child develops fear of water, excessive salivation, confusion, convulsions, or paralysis, rabies is likely and is usually fatal, so prevention now is critical.  
Report the dog to veterinary/public health officers and do not handle its body without protection.
